solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Chewing cud with high-ranking Nazi, as Wallis was?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the title she held, a noun

indicators.note: chewing mashes something up in the mouth, so the letters get churned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Rudolf Hess was Hitler's deputy

explanation.surface: A cow chewing the cud alongside a Nazi grandee, with a nod to Wallis Simpson's notorious Nazi sympathies.
explanation.walkthrough: Wallis Simpson married the abdicated Edward VIII and became Duchess of Windsor; the pair famously met Hitler, which is why Hess fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: After marrying the former king, Wallis Simpson held the title Duchess of Windsor, so the phrase describes her rank.

clue.text: Showy flier's furious, having just one ball

parts.note: flaming means furious, in a raging temper
a single ball is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: A cheeky jibe about a flamboyant pilot who is angry and has only one testicle.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': the flier is furious. 'Just one ball' echoes the old wartime song about Hitler, but here it is simply the round letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: A bright pink wading bird with a flamboyant display that flies, so a showy flier describes it well.

clue.text: Dances at end of jetty — very brave!

parts.note: balls are formal dances

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that last letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone dancing right at the edge of a pier, which looks like a daring thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dances' reads as a verb but is the plural noun: formal balls.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang adjective for daring or gutsy, showing plenty of nerve and courage in a risky situation.

clue.text: Tender PR exponent for e.g. an oil company these days?

definitions.text: e.g. an oil company these days

parts.note: legal tender is money
a public relations expert puts a spin on news, a spin doctor

explanation.surface: A soft-hearted publicist working for an oil giant, a dig at energy firms' image management.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like an adjective (gentle) but is the noun, as in legal tender. The definition is by example: oil firms were making record profits.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that earns large profits reliably; energy companies posted huge windfall gains amid high fuel prices.

clue.text: Hot thing's mound visible in authentic Gucci bottoms

indicators.note: something seen inside another thing sits within it, so one part goes inside the other
in a down clue the bottom of each word is its final letter, so those are kept

parts.note: last letters of the two words
a hill is a mound of earth

explanation.surface: An attractive person's shapely rear showing through genuine Gucci trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot thing' suggests an attractive person and 'bottoms' designer trousers; really it is the spicy pepper, and the bottoms are final letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A chilli pepper is fiery and spicy to eat, so it is literally a hot item of food.

clue.text: Disenchanted with the old political commentator (not doing well at this time)

definitions.text: not doing well at this time
definitions.note: a description of the state, where the answer is a noun for a day of poor form

parts.note: to go off something is to be disenchanted with it
Sir Robin Day was a famous British political interviewer

explanation.surface: Someone disillusioned with a veteran pundit who is currently past his best.
explanation.walkthrough: Robin Day was a combative BBC political interviewer of the 1960s to 80s, hence 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: An off day is a single day when someone performs below their usual standard or feels out of sorts.

clue.text: As delivery drivers do, to share their trials and tribulations

definitions.note: a description of an action, standing for the verb
definitions.meaning: first meaning: take the goods off a van or lorry

definitions.text: to share their trials and tribulations
definitions.meaning: second meaning: pour out one's worries to a listener

explanation.surface: Couriers talking through the hardships of their job, in the style of a gig-economy news story.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs the two senses together as though drivers were confiding in someone; the literal job and the figurative offloading of woes are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Drivers empty their vehicles at each drop, and people figuratively empty out their troubles by confiding them to a friend.

clue.text: Cook said to bring a case against chain, English Forte

indicators.note: something said is spoken rather than written, so we go by the sound of the word

parts.note: to sue someone is to take them to court; the French word is pronounced the same
CH is the abbreviation for chain, an old unit of length
E is the standard abbreviation for English
f is the musical marking for forte, loud

explanation.surface: A legal dispute involving a restaurant chain and the Forte hotel group.
explanation.walkthrough: Forte was a big British hotel and catering group, so 'chain' and 'Forte' look like business names; both are just abbreviations. SOUS in French cooking is pronounced 'soo'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sous-chef is the second-in-command in a professional kitchen, a cook working under the head chef.

clue.text: Treacherous type's sad present

indicators.note: something sad is in a sorry state, so the letters that follow are knocked out of shape

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A traitor's pathetic gift to someone, or perhaps a scheming person's miserable current situation.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': the treacherous type is a rearranged 'present'. 'Sad' reads as an adjective describing the gift.
explanation.definitionFit: A snake in Eden deceived Eve, so the word is a byword for a sly, deceitful or treacherous person.

clue.text: You'll not be proud, putting this away, when screwing Lee with bum, hip

definitions.text: You'll not be proud, putting this away
definitions.note: a description of eating it, standing for the noun

indicators.note: screwing twists something round, so the letters are wrenched into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A saucy Private Eye scene: someone losing all dignity in a romp with a man named Lee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting this away' means eating it, and 'screwing' plays on its crude sense while signalling the twist of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat humble pie is an idiom for admitting you were wrong and swallowing your pride, so a proud person could not do it.

clue.text: A course of conflict resolution and coppers cease to be bent

indicators.note: bent means twisted out of shape, so the letters are bent into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mediation that ends a dispute and also stops the police from being corrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' is British slang for corrupt, which the surface uses of the police; here it just means twisted.
explanation.definitionFit: A series of negotiations and steps between warring sides aimed at ending hostilities is the standard term for this.

clue.text: Did a King Brian and drew the line?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: reigned, like the Irish High King Brian Boru
second meaning: marked a straight line with a ruler

explanation.surface: A monarch called Brian who governed and also set firm limits on what was allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drew the line' sounds like an idiom for refusing; here it is literal, marking a line on paper. Brian Boru was a famous medieval High King of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A king governs his realm, and a person using a straightedge marks lines on paper; both acts share the past tense verb.

clue.text: Ginger wants S&—? In short, yes

parts.note: the ampersand is read as the word it stands for
Y is a short form of yes, as in text messages

explanation.surface: A redhead being asked whether they fancy some S&M, and answering tersely in the affirmative.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash invites the solver to complete 'S&M'; instead the symbol is read out as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandy describes reddish-yellow hair, so it is a synonym for the colour of a redhead's hair.

clue.text: Jeremy Hunt's cure? "Try improvising with a suite"

indicators.note: improvising means making it up on the spot, so the letters are thrown together afresh

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Chancellor's remedy for the economy, quoted as advice to play something by ear.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Hunt was the UK Chancellor of the Exchequer in 2023, and his budgets were accused of a return to spending cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Austerity means tight government spending cuts, the policy critics said the Chancellor prescribed for the ailing economy.

clue.text: Russia's ready to get leader out of difficulty

indicators.note: getting the leader out removes the first in line, so the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: trouble is difficulty

explanation.surface: Russia is prepared to oust Putin to escape its predicament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is not an adjective but British slang for cash, as in 'the ready'. 'Leader' suggests Putin but is just the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The rouble is the Russian currency, and 'the ready' is an informal British term for money or cash.

clue.text: It's painful being less than a top-rated celeb

definitions.note: a description of something sore, standing for a noun
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sore bubble on the skin
second meaning: a second-tier famous person

explanation.surface: The pain of being only a minor celebrity rather than a real star.
explanation.walkthrough: An A-lister is a top celebrity, so the next tier down is a B-lister; the hyphen vanishes in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A fluid-filled bump raised on the skin by rubbing or a burn is sore, and the second sense is a second-rank star.

clue.text: Mean Sunak lives here, figuratively, by day

parts.note: the Prime Minister lives in Number 10 Downing Street, written with the figure as a word
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A mean-spirited Rishi Sunak living somewhere, described loosely, during the daytime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like an insult for Sunak but is the verb. 'Figuratively' hints that the address is a figure, 10, to be spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean to do something is to plan or have it as your purpose, which is exactly what the verb intend expresses.

clue.text: Virgin's shy TV transmission

parts.note: virgin means new, unused
taken as written
to shy is to throw, as at a coconut shy

explanation.surface: A bashful programme broadcast by the Virgin media company.
explanation.walkthrough: Virgin Media is a British TV company, so the capital suggests a brand; 'shy' looks like an adjective but is the verb to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcast of the news on television or radio is a news bulletin, so it is a kind of programme transmitted on air.

clue.text: Crawlers going round ground, etc, making faces

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it, so one part wraps the other

parts.note: asps are snakes, which crawl

indicators.note: ground means crushed up, as coffee is, so the letters are pulverised into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Insects crawling over the ground pulling silly faces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crawlers' suggests insects or toadies, and 'ground' looks like soil; it is past tense of grind. The snakes are split around the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspects and faces are both the different sides or appearances of a question or problem, as in 'many faces of an issue'.

clue.text: What Ukraine must do, tragically, to keep going?

definitions.note: a description of an action, standing for the verb phrase
definitions.meaning: first meaning, literal: keep fighting as soldiers in the war
second meaning, figurative: persevere despite difficulty

explanation.surface: A sombre observation that Ukraine has no choice but to carry on fighting the invasion.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is usually figurative, for pressing on through hardship; for Ukraine it is grimly literal, which is why the clue says 'tragically'.
explanation.definitionFit: To soldier on is an idiom meaning to persevere doggedly, and for a country at war it literally means continuing military resistance.

clue.text: One taking great pleasure in making others smart?

definitions.text: One taking great pleasure in making others smart?

parts.words: One taking great pleasure in making others smart
parts.note: surface reading: a teacher or mentor who loves helping people become clever
setter's reading: smart is the verb to sting, so this person enjoys causing others pain

explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' looks like the adjective clever, but it is the verb meaning to sting or hurt, which turns a kindly tutor into someone cruel.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gets pleasure from inflicting pain on other people is the standard meaning of this word.

clue.text: Live broadcast with vacuous politician is just silliness

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, as seed is sown, so the letters are strewn about

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its insides and only its outer letters remain

parts.note: a Tory politician, with only first and last letters kept

explanation.surface: A live television appearance by an empty-headed MP turns out to be nothing but nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party, the usual crossword politician; emptied, it leaves just its two ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Levity is a lack of seriousness, frivolous or light-hearted behaviour where gravity would be expected.

clue.text: Game requiring guts when energy's lacking

indicators.note: lacking means missing, so the letter this names is taken out

parts.note: guts are the bowels
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A sport that demands courage at moments when you are tired out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guts' suggests courage, but it is the intestines. Bowls is a gentle British lawn game of rolling balls towards a small target ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowls is a sport played on a lawn by rolling weighted balls, so it is simply an example of a game.

clue.text: Outlaw has time in the morning for cock

parts.note: to outlaw something is to ban it
T is the abbreviation for time
a.m. marks times in the morning

explanation.surface: A bandit who makes time at dawn for a rooster, or something ruder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' looks like a noun, a bandit, but it is the verb to ban.
explanation.definitionFit: A bantam is a small breed of domestic chicken, and the male bird of that breed is a cock.

clue.text: It's a sod what a driver might come up with

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a piece of turf

definitions.text: what a driver might come up with
definitions.note: a description standing for the noun
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the chunk of grass a golf club tears up on a shot

explanation.surface: An exasperated grumble about some awkward idea that a motorist might have dreamed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sod' suggests the British curse, and 'driver' a motorist; here the sod is a clump of turf and the driver is a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: A divot is a clod of turf dug out of the grass by a golfer's swing, which is a sod in the old turf sense.

clue.text: Persistent, the French — must be a record

parts.note: a chronic condition persists over a long time
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A dogged French person who must surely have set some kind of record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A record' sounds like a best-ever achievement; here it is a written account.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicle is a written historical account of events in the order they happened, so it is a kind of record.

clue.text: Was an MP possibly one to get up and 'do a Private Eye'

parts.note: an MP sits in Parliament
I is the Roman numeral one
to rise is to get up

explanation.surface: A former MP who might stand up and start mocking the powerful, just as the magazine does.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye, where this puzzle appears, is Britain's leading satirical magazine, so 'doing a Private Eye' means lampooning. MPs are said to sit for their seats.
explanation.definitionFit: The magazine specialises in ridiculing politicians and public figures, so imitating it means to mock through satire.

clue.text: Dog appears with singer on blockbuster movie

parts.note: a bass is a singer with the lowest voice
E.T. was Spielberg's hit 1982 film

explanation.surface: A pet dog turning up in a scene alongside a pop star in a big Hollywood film.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, 'on' means the singer comes first with the film attached after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A basset is a short-legged hound with long ears, a breed of dog originally used for hunting.
